intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil before you read the steps, and answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: What public policy is
sections.big_idea: Public policy is **whatever governments choose to do or not to do**, carried out through a chain of decisions from law to officer's instruction.
in_plain_words: Dye's short definition includes laws, spending and the choice to leave a problem alone. The working definition adds two tests: a choice among options, and the authority of the state to command, spend, inform or organise. Policy lives in several documents at once, each with its own legal force.

Governments act for reasons such as public goods, externalities, information gaps and rights, and the reason shapes the tool. Many actors share power, and every policy trades values such as efficiency and equity. Deciding not to act is also a policy, so list what a government has not done.

diagram.caption: the chain from Cabinet room to ration shop

key_terms.meaning: A course of action or deliberate inaction by a public authority.
Binding law that creates rights, duties and institutions.
A plan of spending and delivery, often made under an Act.
An issue that never reaches a formal decision.
A cost or benefit that falls on others.

worked_example.title: Which document creates the right?
worked_example.setup: Take the rural employment guarantee as the example. Sort four documents by what each does.
steps: The VB-G RAM G Act 2025, s5, creates the entitlement: 125 days of guaranteed work a year.
Rules under the Act add detail made by the executive.
The State Scheme, notified within six months (s3), describes how the guarantee is delivered.
That answer decides what a citizen can enforce.
worked_example.answer: The Act creates the right; the rules and the Scheme describe how it is delivered.

mistakes: Reading only the scheme guidelines and missing the Act that creates the entitlement.
Treating inaction as no policy. Leaving a law without rules is a choice with consequences.
Assuming a reason for public action proves the programme will work.

recall.q: Who wrote the most quoted definition of public policy?
recall.a: Thomas Dye, in Understanding Public Policy (1972): whatever governments choose to do or not to do.

recall.q: Name the two tests in the working definition.
recall.a: Choice among options, and authority backed by the state's power.

recall.q: Give two reasons a problem becomes a public responsibility.
recall.a: Any two of: public goods, externalities, information gaps, equity and rights.

recall.q: What is visible inaction?
recall.a: For example a law with no rules notified, or a bill left to lapse.

recall.q: Which trade does the biometric ration example show?
recall.a: Leakage control (efficiency) against turning away eligible families (equity).

sections.title: The policy cycle
sections.big_idea: The five-stage cycle is a **shared map**: agenda, formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation. It organises analysis but does not describe how policy really moves.
in_plain_words: Lasswell's seven functions were condensed into five stages. Agenda setting gets an issue official attention, formulation designs options inside government, adoption is the decision by an authority with legal power, implementation is what officials do, and evaluation judges results and feeds them back.

Each stage has its own actors and openings. The cycle helps you locate a policy and plan engagement, but stages overlap and implementation can reshape the policy. The worked mapping of MGNREGA to VB-G RAM G shows each stage in public documents, and shows that outcome evidence does not yet exist.

diagram.caption: five stages, rarely in clean order

key_terms.meaning: The stage when a problem gains official attention.
Issues a Cabinet, legislature or court is actually considering.
Turning a problem into a proposal inside government.
A decision by an authority with legal power.
NITI Aayog's evaluation office, constituted in September 2015.

worked_example.title: Map a change onto the cycle
worked_example.setup: Use the replacement of NREGA 2005 by the VB-G RAM G Act 2025.
steps: Earlier policy: NREGA 2005 guaranteed at least 100 days a year (s3).
Adoption: the VB-G RAM G Act, Act No. 36 of 2025, dated 20 December 2025.
Commencement: S.O. 2382(E) of 11 May 2026 brought it into force from 1 July 2026.
Implementation: States notify Schemes within six months (s3).
Evaluation: too early for outcome evidence as of October 2026.
worked_example.answer: Every stage is documented except evaluation, which has no evidence yet.

mistakes: Reading the cycle as a description of how policy moves, when stages overlap and decisions are revisited.
Writing a claim about the new Act's effects before a full year of data exists.
Treating the official decision as the end of the politics.

recall.q: Who divided the decision process into seven functions?
recall.a: Harold Lasswell, in 1956.

recall.q: What is the difference between public and institutional agenda?
recall.a: The public agenda is what people talk about; the institutional agenda is what a Cabinet, legislature or court is considering.

recall.q: Which article makes the Council of Ministers advise the President?
recall.a: Article 74(1).

recall.q: What does evaluation need to be useful?
recall.a: To reach the next decision, for example by linking scheme renewal to evaluation.

recall.q: Name two uses of the cycle.
recall.a: For example locate where a policy is, plan who to engage, design an evaluation, structure a brief.

sections.title: Theories that complicate the cycle
sections.big_idea: Three theories correct the cycle: **small steps, timing and sudden change**. Each gives you a different question to ask of a policy problem.
in_plain_words: The rational model assumes clear goals, every option listed and one decision maker, which no ministry has. Lindblom's incrementalism describes small steps from current policy, which suits budgets and favours the status quo. Kingdon's multiple streams explain timing: problem, policy and politics join in a window.

Baumgartner and Jones explain long calm and sudden change through policy image and venue. The right to food moving to the Supreme Court is a venue shift. None of the theories is right alone, and political economy adds the question none of them asks: who gains, who loses, and what will they do about it.

events.what: Lasswell's seven functions, the cycle's source

diagram.caption: four ways to explain policy change

key_terms.meaning: Assumes clear goals, all options listed and reliable predictions.
Decisions as small changes from current policy.
Moment when problem, policy and politics streams can join.
Person who couples a ready solution to a recognised problem.
How an issue is portrayed and understood.
The institution where an issue is decided.

worked_example.title: The incremental budget
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures from the slide, in Rs crore. Check the stated changes.
steps: Scheme A rises from 1,000 to 1,060: 1,060 − 1,000 = 60.
As a share of last year's budget: 60 ÷ 1,000 = 6%.
Scheme B rises from 400 to 420: 420 − 400 = 20.
As a share: 20 ÷ 400 = 5%.
Scheme C is a new pilot of 25 and Scheme D stays at 300, so nothing is cut.
worked_example.answer: Established lines move 5 to 6 per cent and a small new pilot line appears.

mistakes: Expecting an evaluation that shows failure to cut a budget. It more often changes the design.
Arriving at a policy window without a worked-out solution.
Treating one theory as the whole explanation.

recall.q: Who wrote 'The Science of Muddling Through' and when?
recall.a: Charles Lindblom, in 1959.

recall.q: Name Kingdon's three streams.
recall.a: Problem, policy and politics.

recall.q: What do Baumgartner and Jones say changes when an issue moves?
recall.a: The policy image and the venue.

recall.q: What did the 28 November 2001 order change?
recall.a: The right to food moved from state departments to the Supreme Court, which kept monitoring compliance.

recall.q: What question does political economy add?
recall.a: Who gains and who loses, and what will they do about it.

sections.title: Policy instruments
sections.big_idea: Every tool draws on **nodality, authority, treasure or organisation**. Choose from a diagnosis of why the problem exists and plan for the main risk.
in_plain_words: Hood grouped tools by resource: information, legal power, money and the state's own people and buildings. Instruments run from laissez faire through nudge and incentivise to mandate, and stronger tools cost more to enforce and restrict more choice. Regulation shifts cost to inspection and enforcement.

Subsidies and transfers raise questions of who benefits and how delivery works, and conditions need verification and a supplied service. Information and nudges rely on norms, defaults and reminders. Match the instrument to the cause and name the main risk: exclusion errors, weak enforcement, ignored messages, silent exclusion.

diagram.caption: NATO: every tool uses at least one

key_terms.meaning: Being at the centre of information networks.
Money or exchangeable assets.
Changing how a choice is presented without forbidding anything.
The option that applies if a person does nothing.
Cash paid only if the household does something.

worked_example.title: Match the instrument to the cause
worked_example.setup: Use the table on the slide Choosing for three diagnoses.
steps: Poor households lack money: consider cash or in-kind transfers, and plan for exclusion errors in targeting.
Harm imposed on others: consider regulation or taxes, and plan for weak enforcement and evasion.
Inertia or forgetting: consider defaults or reminders, and plan for small effects and silent exclusion.
worked_example.answer: Transfers, regulation and taxes, then defaults; each with its named risk.

mistakes: Treating a stronger tool as a better tool. Stronger tools cost more to enforce and restrict more choice.
Conditioning a payment on a service the state cannot supply.
Counting subsidy savings without asking who the default or the cut leaves out.

recall.q: What does NATO stand for in Hood's scheme?
recall.a: Nodality, authority, treasure and organisation.

recall.q: Which levels sit on the Economic Survey 2018-19 spectrum?
recall.a: Laissez faire, nudge, incentivise and mandate.

recall.q: What is the design rule for conditional transfers?
recall.a: Never condition a payment on a service the state cannot supply.

recall.q: Why did the Give It Up campaign reach limits?
recall.a: It relied on opt-in, so inertia kept most better-off households in the scheme.

recall.q: What does the plastic ban rely on for its start date?
recall.a: A start date announced about ten months ahead, with alternatives available.

sections.title: How policy is made in India
sections.big_idea: Learn the **rules of the file**: who owns it, who must be consulted, where Cabinet and Parliament enter, and which list the subject sits on.
in_plain_words: The Constitution makes the Council of Ministers advise the President, and two sets of rules turn that into practice. Allocation of Business assigns subjects to ministries, Transaction of Business sets who is consulted and which cases reach Cabinet. Finance and Law shape drafts before anyone outside sees them.

Bills pass through Parliament, where committee scrutiny now covers few bills. The Seventh Schedule and Centrally Sponsored Schemes mean states carry most social policy and part of its cost. Courts act through PILs and review policy. NITI Aayog and the 2014 consultation policy rest on executive decisions.

diagram.root: How policy is made in India
diagram.caption: four places where policy is made

key_terms.meaning: Rules on consultation and which cases reach Cabinet.
Rules listing ministries and allotting every subject to one.
Cases that must go to the full Cabinet.
Subjects on which Union and states both legislate.
Public interest litigation, relaxing who may sue.

worked_example.title: Trace a proposal through the rules
worked_example.setup: A ministry drafts a bill that has a financial bearing and concerns another department.
steps: The owning ministry drafts it. Other affected departments are consulted (rule 4(1)).
The Ministry of Finance must concur because of the financial bearing (rule 4(2)).
The Ministry of Law is consulted because it is a proposal for legislation (rule 4(3)).
Cases involving legislation go to the full Cabinet (Second Schedule).
Then it goes to Parliament and to the President for assent.
worked_example.answer: Ministry, other departments, Finance, Law, Cabinet, Parliament, President.

mistakes: Writing to the minister when the file sits with another officer.
Assuming the 2014 consultation policy binds like a statute. It is an executive policy with no statute behind it.
Overlooking that only 16% of bills went to committees in the 17th Lok Sabha.

recall.q: Which article provides for the Council of Ministers?
recall.a: Article 74(1).

recall.q: How long is the comment window under the 2014 consultation policy?
recall.a: 30 days.

recall.q: Which list holds police and public health?
recall.a: The State List.

recall.q: What is the usual funding split for most states under the VB-G RAM G Act?
recall.a: 60:40, Union to State.

recall.q: What did the 42nd Amendment change?
recall.a: It moved education from the State List to the Concurrent List in 1976.

sections.title: Implementation and state capacity
sections.big_idea: Implementation is where policy happens. **Count the steps, name the frontline worker, and measure exclusion** as well as leakage.
in_plain_words: Pressman and Wildavsky showed how a chain of agreements gives many chances to stall. Top-down views ask why officials departed from the law, and bottom-up views start at the frontline. Lipsky's street-level bureaucrats cope with too many cases through routines that become the policy as performed.

Pritchett's flailing state separates de jure from de facto, Kapur sees success on large tasks and failure on local ones, and Dasgupta and Kapur show overload. Absence studies measure the gap. The lesson is to design for delivery: count approvals, budget for staff, plan grievances, pilot in a hard district.

left.title: Top-down view
items: Fix: clearer goals, fewer veto points

right.title: Bottom-up view
items: Ask how officials and citizens behave

diagram.caption: two ways to look at the gap

key_terms.meaning: The distance between a policy's promise and delivery.
Frontline worker with discretion over citizens.
Rationing, creaming or referral used to manage demand.
What rules say against what happens.
Officials heavily under-resourced for their responsibilities.

worked_example.title: Why many clearances stall
worked_example.setup: Illustrative, from the slide. A scheme needs several separate clearances, each with a 90% chance of coming through on time.
steps: Two clearances: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81.
Three clearances: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729.
Keep multiplying by 0.9 and the chance falls steadily.
For ten clearances the chance that all arrive on time is about 35%.
worked_example.answer: Each added clearance lowers the odds; ten clearances at 90% give about 35%.

mistakes: Believing a pilot's results will hold at scale without checking delivery capacity.
Counting leakage savings and never counting exclusion.
Blaming rent-seeking alone when officials may simply be overloaded.

recall.q: Who wrote Implementation (1973)?
recall.a: Jeffrey Pressman and Aaron Wildavsky.

recall.q: What did Lipsky's frontline workers share?
recall.a: Too few resources, rising demand, vague goals and clients who cannot go elsewhere.

recall.q: What test does Pritchett's idea suggest for a scheme?
recall.a: Collect one rule and one observation of practice, then compare them.

recall.q: What did unannounced visits find about teacher absence?
recall.a: About 25% absent in one study and 23.6% in a later Indian panel.

recall.q: Name two items from the delivery checklist.
recall.a: For example count the steps between money and citizen, or pilot in a hard district.

sections.title: Evidence in policy
sections.big_idea: Match the evidence to the decision. **Read every headline saving as a claim to test**, and plan for the wait until a decision window opens.
in_plain_words: Kinds of evidence answer different questions: trials, administrative data, surveys, qualitative work and audits. Trials built into rollouts show what a reform did. In Andhra Pradesh, Smartcards made payments faster without cutting access, while in Jharkhand authentication cut corruption but cost eligible people access.

Government claims of savings need questions about definition, counterfactual and who was excluded. DMEO offers tools and sector evaluations. Personal data brings the DPDP Act duties from 13 May 2027, with a research exemption. Evidence reaches decisions when it answers a question already being asked, at the time of decision.

key_terms.meaning: What would have happened without the policy.
Records such as MIS and payment data.
Eligible people turned away.
Evaluates central schemes; runs OOMF and DGQI.
Section 17(2)(b): research use if no individual decisions follow.

worked_example.title: Test a savings claim
worked_example.setup: A press note reports Rs 3.48 lakh crore of cumulative DBT savings, of which Rs 1.85 lakh crore came from food subsidies.
steps: Share from food subsidies: 1.85 ÷ 3.48 = 53%.
Ask how a 'saving' is defined and against what counterfactual.
Ask whether deleted ration cards were ineligible, duplicate or eligible people excluded.
Ask whether 176 crore beneficiaries counts people, accounts or transactions.
worked_example.answer: Just over half comes from food subsidies, so the exclusion question matters most.

mistakes: Quoting a figure with no year or source.
Reading a technology result from one design as true for another. The same technology helped in one design and harmed in another.
Producing a report after the budget is set.

recall.q: How was the Andhra Pradesh Smartcards rollout randomised?
recall.a: Across 157 subdistricts covering 19 million people.

recall.q: What happened to access in Jharkhand?
recall.a: 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point.

recall.q: What is OOMF?
recall.a: DMEO's Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework.

recall.q: From when do the DPDP duties apply?
Name one step for getting evidence used.
recall.a: For example agree in advance what result would change the decision.

sections.title: South Asian cases
sections.big_idea: Four cases teach recurring lessons: **funding rules shape provision, targeting is political, technology depends on design, and opaque formulas exclude**.
in_plain_words: The rural employment guarantee shows a statute rewritten. NREGA 2005 gave a hundred days and a Union-funded wage bill. The VB-G RAM G Act raises the guarantee to 125 days, shares wage costs, caps spending at an allocation, adds a seasonal pause and links works to panchayat plans. No outcome data exists yet.

The Aadhaar Act, BISP and Aswesuma add three lessons. Technology helps or harms through design and rollout, and exclusion must be tracked like leakage. Targeting is political: who identifies the poor controls the programme. A formula can exclude when its weights and cut-off are not public. Courts set floors while states deliver.

events.what: VB-G RAM G Act in force

key_terms.meaning: A Union-set allocation per state; spending above it falls on the state.
The more work demanded, the more the Union must fund.
Scoring households on indicators correlated with poverty.
Sri Lanka's welfare benefit that replaced Samurdhi in 2023.
Bill type the majority held the Aadhaar Act was rightly passed as.

worked_example.title: Who pays under the new Act?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. Rs 100 of wage cost falls within a state's normative allocation.
steps: Guarantee: 125 − 100 = 25 more days than under NREGA 2005.
At 60:40 the Union pays 100 × 0.6 = 60.
The state pays 100 × 0.4 = 40.
At 90:10 the Union pays 100 × 0.9 = 90, the state 100 × 0.1 = 10.
Spending above the allocation is borne by the state.
worked_example.answer: 25 more days; the Union pays 60 or 90 of each 100, within the allocation.

mistakes: Quoting the new Act's effect without outcome data from a full financial year.
Treating a scorecard as neutral when who designs it decides who controls the benefits.
Assuming a court order guarantees delivery when states must still comply.

recall.q: How many days does NREGA 2005 guarantee?
recall.a: Not less than one hundred days a year (s3).

recall.q: What is the seasonal pause in the new Act?
recall.a: Sixty days a year in aggregate, notified by states (s6).

recall.q: What did Puttaswamy uphold and strike down?
recall.a: It upheld section 7 and struck down the part of section 57 allowing private authentication.

recall.q: How did BISP change targeting?
recall.a: A poverty scorecard based on a proxy means test replaced selection by legislators' forms.

recall.q: What did the Aswesuma appraisal say about transparency?
recall.a: The weights and cut-off score were not public.

sections.title: Stakeholders and political economy
sections.big_idea: Well-designed policies fail when losers are organised and gainers scattered. **Ask who decides, gains and loses**, and test feasibility on four fronts.
in_plain_words: Political economy looks at interests, institutions and incentives. Problem-driven analysis defines the problem, examines governance, and then examines drivers. A power and interest grid places stakeholders and tells you whom to engage closely or keep informed. Concentrated costs with diffuse benefits usually favour the small organised group.

Shared schemes add a Centre and state with different incentives. Before recommending, test technical, political, administrative and financial feasibility and write down the evidence. Timing matters too: prepare evidence, a costed proposal and allies so you are ready when a window opens.

key_terms.meaning: Study of interests, institutions and incentives behind a problem.
Costs borne by a small organised group.
Grid placing actors by power and interest.
Technical, political, administrative and financial tests.
A moment when change becomes possible.

worked_example.title: Place the plastic-ban stakeholders
worked_example.setup: Use the invented example. Place four actors on the grid.
steps: Plastic manufacturers' associations: high power, high interest. Engage closely and early.
State finance departments: high power, low interest. Keep satisfied.
Waste pickers: low power, high interest. Organise and consult.
Most consumers: low power, low interest. Inform, since their behaviour decides whether the ban works.
worked_example.answer: Close engagement, keep satisfied, organise and consult, inform.

mistakes: Treating a technically best option as one that will be adopted.
Skipping the administrative feasibility test, which Sections 6 and 8 show failing most often.
Arriving at a window with no evidence, costed proposal or draft text.

recall.q: What are the two questions in political economy versus technical analysis?
recall.a: Technical: what works best. Political economy: who decides, gains, loses and what can each do.

recall.q: What are the three steps in problem-driven analysis?
recall.a: Define the problem, examine governance and institutions, examine drivers: interests, incentives, power.

recall.q: What does a 60:40 split mean for a state?
recall.a: It pays two rupees for every three the Union pays.

recall.q: Name the four feasibility tests.
recall.a: Technical, political, administrative, financial.

recall.q: Name two signals that a window may open.
recall.a: For example a new government, a budget cycle, a court hearing, a crisis, a new survey.

sections.title: A practitioner's toolkit
sections.big_idea: A six-step analysis, a document checklist and a monitoring plan keep practice honest. **State criteria first, include the status quo, and monitor exclusion.**
in_plain_words: Policy analysis advises a decision maker: define the problem with evidence of its size, set criteria, build three or four options including the status quo, project outcomes and costs, compare trade-offs and recommend, saying what would change your mind. Choosing criteria after seeing results invites bias.

Before acting on a policy, assemble all its documents: Act, rules, Scheme, guidelines, budget, court orders, committee reports and evaluations, and talk to a frontline official. Engage at each stage by its formal route, and monitor the risks the case studies show, with legal deadlines as natural indicators.

nodes.label: Build options
nodes.sub: three or four, with status quo

diagram.caption: six steps of a policy analysis

key_terms.meaning: 'No change' analysed as an option with its own costs.
Standards for judging options, set first.
Scoring options against criteria and weights.
A signal that a monitored risk is arising.
A request for information under the Right to Information Act 2005.

worked_example.title: Scores are not the decision
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scores on four criteria (exclusion, leakage, cost, feasibility) from the options table.
steps: Status quo: 1 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 10.
One-time password: 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 9.
Manual override: 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 9.
Combined nominee and audited override: 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9.
worked_example.answer: Totals sit at 9 or 10, so the decision rests on weights that must be stated openly.

mistakes: Treating a scheme guideline as the law.
Ignoring the status quo option.
Writing to the minister when the file sits with another officer, or asking for everything at once.

recall.q: What are the six steps of policy analysis?
recall.a: Define the problem, set criteria, build options, project outcomes and costs, compare trade-offs, recommend.

recall.q: Why state criteria first?
recall.a: Choosing them after seeing results invites bias toward a favoured option.

recall.q: Name the formal routes for engaging at the implementation stage.
recall.a: RTI requests, grievance systems and social audits.

recall.q: What are the legal deadlines under VB-G RAM G?
recall.a: Wages within a fortnight (s5(3)) and work within fifteen days of an application (s11).

recall.q: What habit prevents most mistakes?
recall.a: Writing down the decision, the person and the date before starting.

sections.title: Writing a policy brief, and where next
sections.big_idea: A brief tells a named decision maker **what to do**. Put the finding first, source every number, state limits plainly and label what you invented.
in_plain_words: A brief is two to four pages for a reader with little time and a decision to make. Answer three questions first: who reads it, what decision they face, what you want them to do. Put the conclusion first, with a title that states the finding and a summary in 100 words.

Write plainly: lead with the point, give every number its source and year, use the active voice and name who must act. Say what kind of study produced a number and state its main limit once. Prefer one strong study you can describe. Label invented examples and date claims that can change.

right.title: Policy brief
items: Written for a named decision maker
Judged on whether it is used

key_terms.meaning: A short document for a decision maker with a decision to make.
A title that states the finding.
Problem, finding and recommendation in 100 words.
Label for an invented example.
Names who must act.

worked_example.title: Rewrite a weak title
worked_example.setup: The weak title reads 'An analysis of authentication in the public distribution system'.
steps: Spot the problem: it names a topic and gives no finding.
State the finding: fingerprint failures are excluding eligible families.
Add the action: a nominee rule would fix most cases.
The new title: 'Fingerprint failures are excluding eligible families; a nominee rule would fix most cases'.
worked_example.answer: A finding-first title that tells the reader what to do.

mistakes: Writing a brief like a research paper, with the answer at the end.
Overstating certainty. Readers forgive uncertainty that is explained.
Citing a number with no source or year.

recall.q: What three questions come before writing a brief?
recall.a: Who will read it, what decision they face, what you want them to do.

recall.q: How long is a summary?
recall.a: 100 words.

recall.q: What should every number carry?
recall.a: Its source and year.

recall.q: Which course is the next step if implementation is your concern?
recall.a: Governance & Accountability 101.

recall.q: How should an invented example be marked?
recall.a: As illustrative.

notes.2: Use the agenda to see the arc: what policy is, the cycle, the theories that complicate it, instruments, the Indian process, implementation, evidence, cases, politics, tools and writing. **Section 6 on implementation matters most to practitioners**, since slide 16 calls it where most policies succeed or fail. Read in order the first time.
notes.4: Start with the three pictures: a thumbprint at a ration shop, a school meal, a banned carry bag. Each is the end of a **chain of public decisions**. Notice the dating warning at the foot: facts are stated as of October 2026, so check the latest text before relying on any scheme, number or law.
notes.5: Memorise Dye's line, then spot its weakness: it counts almost anything a government does. The working definition adds two tests, **choice and authority**. Use them to decide whether something is policy. Remember that deliberate inaction counts, which the next slides develop.
notes.6: One policy usually lives in several documents with different legal force. Use the table as a checklist for any subject. The question at the foot decides what a citizen can enforce: **which document creates the right, and which only describes delivery?** Read the Act before the scheme guidelines.
notes.7: These four reasons are grounds to consider public action, and none proves a programme will beat doing nothing, which later sections test. Match reason to tool: **a rights argument points to an entitlement law, an externality argument to a tax or a ban**. Ask which reason a government actually gave.
notes.8: Record what a government has not done as carefully as what it has done. Visible inaction leaves traces, such as rules never notified or bills allowed to lapse. Invisible inaction leaves none, because no file is opened. **Gaps are often where advocacy and research add most**, so list them early.
notes.9: Map actors by their main lever. The table pairs each actor with a lever and an example you will meet again. **Formal authority and real influence differ**, so add the bureaucracy, donors, business, civil society and the media to the picture. Section 9 turns this into a mapping method.
notes.10: Treat every policy as a trade between goods, such as speed against care or efficiency against equity. The six value words give you a vocabulary for naming the trade. The ration example shows it: **leakage control (efficiency) against turning away eligible families (equity)**. Ask which value a proposal protects.
notes.12: Learn the five stages as a shared vocabulary: agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation. Lasswell's seven functions came first. Its strength is a **common map for ministries, donors and evaluators**, and its weakness is that real policy rarely moves in order. Use it to ask where a policy sits.
notes.13: Separate the public agenda from the institutional agenda. Most advocacy tries to **move an issue from the first to the second**. Use the six routes in the list as prompts for your own issue. The 2001 midday meal order shows a court putting an issue on every state's agenda at once.
notes.14: Formulation happens inside government, and the consultation rules explain why drafts change before outsiders see them. Use the table to predict who will comment on your proposal: Finance on cost, Law on legal form. **Cost and fiscal space shape what survives**, so prepare a cost estimate early.
notes.15: Follow the route for a bill: ministry drafts, Cabinet approves, Parliament passes, the President assents, then rules and schemes follow. **New rights and duties need an Act**, while schemes and many rules need only the executive. Ask which route your policy took, since that decides how easily it can change.
notes.16: Implementation is the stage where policy actually happens. The VB-G RAM G Act shows the division of labour: Union framework, State Scheme within six months, Panchayat planning. Use the six-actor list to find who can **delay money or hide an entitlement**. Design for implementation from the first draft.
notes.17: Evaluation matters only if it reaches the next decision. Note DMEO's origin in 2015 as a merger of two evaluation offices, and its use in the Finance Commission cycle. **Linking scheme renewal to evaluation** is one way to force results into a decision. Find the next decision point before you start.
notes.18: Use this mapping as a template: for any change, list what happened at each stage and cite the document. The row to remember is the last one. **There is no outcome evidence yet**, and the slide says to treat claims about the new Act's effects with care until a full financial year of data exists.
notes.19: Use the cycle to organise analysis and monitoring, and avoid reading it as a description of how policy moves. Stages overlap and implementation reshapes policy. The two columns work as a checklist of uses and misuses. **The official decision does not end the politics**, as the next section's theories show.
notes.21: The rational model is a benchmark. It assumes clear goals, every option listed, reliable predictions and one decision maker, and **no ministry has that time, information or agreement**. Use the right-hand column as a list of the constraints to expect: contested goals, patchy data, many vetoes.
notes.22: Remember Lindblom as small steps from current policy: few options, reversible mistakes, easier agreement. The critique matters for advocacy, since **small steps favour the status quo** and those it already serves. When your problem needs a large change, expect incrementalism to delay it and plan for a window.
notes.23: Read the invented budget as a lesson in odds. Established lines move by a few per cent, a new pilot appears as a small new line, and nothing is cut. For practitioners, **a small new line has better odds than a proposal that needs cuts**. For evaluators, evidence of failure more often changes a design than a budget.
notes.24: Hold Kingdon's three streams as problem, policy and politics, joined by a policy entrepreneur when a window opens. His practical lesson is for you: **have a worked-out solution ready before the window opens**, because windows close quickly. Ask which stream your own issue is missing.
notes.25: The 1991 reforms illustrate a window, and the slide labels the mapping as interpretation. Use the method: separate **problem, available ideas and politics**, then ask what joined them. Apply the same three questions to a reform you are studying, and look for who coupled the streams.
notes.26: Punctuated equilibrium explains long calm followed by sudden shift. A small policy community keeps an issue technical, and change comes when the **image is redefined and the venue moves**. Ask two questions of your issue: how is it portrayed, and where is it decided? Excluded groups may go venue shopping.
notes.27: The midday meal case shows a venue shift: from state departments to the Supreme Court, and from welfare scheme to constitutional right. The 2003 order shows its limit, since Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh had not begun. **A new venue changes the decision; delivery still depends on states.**
notes.28: Use the table to pick the right lens. Each theory explains something and misses something, so combine them. The last column gives you one question per theory to bring to a meeting. The footer adds the missing question for all four: **who gains, who loses, and what will they do about it?**
notes.30: Remember NATO: nodality, authority, treasure, organisation. Every instrument draws on at least one. The quick diagnostic at the foot is to ask **which resource a scheme relies on and whether the state has enough of it**. Try it on a scheme you work with, using the table's examples.
notes.31: Place a policy on the spectrum from laissez faire through nudge and incentivise to mandate. The Survey's examples are discussion questions, since placements can be argued. The principle at the foot is useful: **stronger tools are not better tools**, because they cost more to enforce and restrict more choice.
notes.32: Regulation looks cheap, yet its real cost sits in inspection and enforcement. The plastic ban worked on a clear list, an announced start date and available alternatives. It weakens with thousands of small sellers and thin enforcement. **Check whether the enforcing body has the staff** before relying on a ban.
notes.33: Read the chart as leakage by commodity. The other findings concern who benefits from price subsidies: the bottom half of households consumed only 25 per cent of LPG, and the top electricity quintile captured far more than the bottom. **Universal-looking subsidies often favour heavy consumers.** Check the source table before quoting.
notes.34: Compare cash and in-kind on the table, and notice each has its own risks. In-kind guarantees a good but needs a supply chain; cash is cheaper and gives choice but needs bank access. **The evidence on DBT in India is more mixed** than either side of the debate usually admits, as Section 8 shows.
notes.35: Conditions link cash to services, but someone must verify compliance and the poorest may find it hardest to comply. The design rule is the one to memorise: **never condition a payment on a service the state cannot supply**. BISP shows both types running side by side in one programme.
notes.36: Give It Up shows persuasion using nodality: low cost, social norms, and a link to a BPL household's LPG connection. The limit is opt-in, because **inertia keeps most better-off households in the scheme**. The Economic Survey suggested making the default opt-out. Check the totals against their dated sources.
notes.37: A nudge changes how a choice is presented. The three principles are social norms, defaults and repeated reminders. A default can move behaviour more than a subsidy. The caution deserves a check: **an automatic enrolment can exclude people if the system behind it fails**, so ask who the default leaves out.
notes.38: Pick an instrument from a diagnosis of why the problem exists, then name the main risk before it arrives. Use the table row by row: cause, instrument, risk. **Instruments are often combined**, and the VB-G RAM G Act mixes wages, a legal guarantee and panchayat-run works.
notes.40: Learn the two sets of rules: Allocation of Business assigns subjects to ministries, and Transaction of Business sets how business is done. Together they tell you **which officer holds the file on your issue**, which is where serious engagement with government begins. The executive acts in the President's name on the government's decisions.
notes.41: Follow the path of a note: owning department, other departments, Finance and Law, the minister, then Cabinet where rules require it. The detail to remember is **Finance concurrence**, where many ambitious proposals are scaled down. Prepare an early cost estimate, because it improves a proposal's chance of surviving.
notes.42: Know which cases must reach the full Cabinet, such as legislation and the appointment of commissions. Commissions are a common way to defer or prepare reform, so watch for one. Rule 6(7) is a useful detail: **a case touching several departments waits until all are consulted** before a Cabinet committee sees it.
notes.43: Contrast the two bodies: the Planning Commission drew up Five-Year Plans, while NITI Aayog advises through indices and strategy papers. Both rest on resolutions, so **a later government can change them without amending any law**. Remember that NITI houses DMEO as an attached office.
notes.44: The 2014 consultation policy gives a 30-day window for comment on draft bills, with justification and impact assessment. Use it: **any organisation can comment before the Cabinet approves**, when change is cheapest. Its weakness is that it is executive policy with no statute behind it, and PRS found uneven application.
notes.45: Walk a bill through five steps and mark where you can engage. Committees invite written submissions and sometimes oral evidence. The warning concerns time: **in the 15th Lok Sabha, 35% of bills passed were debated for an hour or less**. Referral to a committee is not mandatory.
notes.46: The chart shows committee referral falling, to 16% in the 17th Lok Sabha. Committees remain active, with about 1,700 meetings, so **unreferred bills miss scrutiny that is still available**. If a bill matters to you, ask early whether it will be referred and prepare a memo anyway.
notes.47: Use the Seventh Schedule to find who may legislate on your subject. Police, public health and agriculture are State List; education moved to the Concurrent List in 1976. Because much social policy sits with states or in the Concurrent List, **national schemes depend on state governments**. Check the list before choosing a target.
notes.48: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are designed and part-funded by the Union and carried out by states, so the funding formula is a policy choice. Read the split: 60:40 for most states and 90:10 for the North Eastern and Himalayan States and J&K. **Spending above the normative allocation falls on the state.**
notes.49: Courts act as policy makers through PILs. The relaxed standing rule is why one petition can reshape midday meals or undertrial detention. Weigh the criticism too: courts lack budgets, staff and field knowledge, and orders can be hard to enforce. Courts also **review policy**, as in the Aadhaar judgment.
notes.51: Implementation is where promises weaken. Compare the top-down and bottom-up views, which ask different questions. The arithmetic makes the point: **ten clearances at 90% each leave only about 35%** for all to arrive on time. Count the approvals between money and citizen in any design you review.
notes.52: Lipsky's insight is that frontline workers make policy in practice, through routines and rationing. Name the street-level bureaucrats in your own scheme: anganwadi workers, ASHAs, teachers, ration dealers. **To know what a policy is, watch what these officials do** as well as reading the law.
notes.53: The coping routines are invented examples of mechanisms: rationing, creaming, referral, gatekeeping. Learn the pattern in the third column, where each routine changes who gets the policy. The design response has three parts: **reduce harmful discretion, resource helpful discretion, and measure who is turned away**.
notes.54: Pritchett's test is practical: pick a scheme, collect one rule and one observation of practice, and compare. The distinction to hold is **de jure against de facto**, what the rules say against what happens in the clinic, school and licence office. Keep a written pair for every scheme you study.
notes.55: Kapur's picture is mixed: the state delivers on episodic, large-scale and macroeconomic tasks and falters on daily local services. Use the table to ask which side your scheme falls on. His three reasons are under-resourced local governments, early democracy and social cleavage, and he finds **micro-level capacity improving**.
notes.56: Choose between two explanations of poor delivery. If officials are captured, add control and vigilance; if they are overloaded, add staff, cut paperwork and clarify priorities. The survey evidence links fewer resources to worse implementation. Note the link to elections: **fewer resources go where responsibility is unclear**.
notes.57: Unannounced visits measure implementation directly. The figures show teacher absence of 25% in one study and 23.6% in a later panel, with an estimated annual salary cost of $1.5 bn. The sting is cost-effectiveness: **more frequent monitoring could be over ten times more effective** than hiring more teachers.
notes.58: Use the checklist on any draft scheme before adoption. The first two items catch most trouble: count the steps between money and citizen, and name the frontline worker. **Measure exclusion as well as leakage**, and publish the data that would show the scheme failing. Pilot in a hard district first.
notes.60: Match evidence to the question. Trials say whether a policy caused change, administrative data say who was reached, surveys say how common, qualitative work says why, and audits say whether money was spent as claimed. **The best evidence answers the decision's question.** Check the 'watch for' column before relying on a source.
notes.61: The Andhra Pradesh Smartcards study is the model of a trial built into a rollout: the order of areas was randomised across 157 subdistricts. Results: faster payments, less leakage, no fall in access, and strong preference for the new system. **A large experiment can sit inside a real government rollout.**
notes.62: The just-in-time funds reform cut expenditure by 24% in the experiment and 19% after scale-up, with officials' personal wealth down 10%. Read the closing line: **payment delays increased**. Good evaluations report the costs of a reform alongside its gains, and you should look for both.
notes.63: Hold this beside the Andhra Pradesh result. In Jharkhand, Aadhaar-based authentication cut corruption but 1.5–2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point. The authors read the harm as driven mainly by how the transition was managed, so **the same broad technology helped in one design and harmed in another**.
notes.64: Read official savings claims with the question column in hand. Ask how a saving is defined and against what counterfactual, whether deleted cards were ineligible or eligible, and whether coverage figures count people, accounts or transactions. **Treat a headline saving as a claim to test**, and read it with the Jharkhand evidence.
notes.65: Before designing an evaluation of a central scheme, check whether DMEO has already evaluated it, and use its indicators so your findings compare. The two tools are OOMF, which maps outlays to outputs and outcomes, and DGQI, which reviews data preparedness. The sources are DMEO pages, so **check current versions**.
notes.66: Treat the DPDP research exemption as a checklist: confirm your purpose is research or statistics, use no data to decide about an individual, follow the prescribed standards, minimise, separate identifiers. **The duties apply from 13 May 2027**, so date your own project against it. The Data Protection course has the detail.
notes.67: A strong evaluation is one input competing with budgets and promises. Use the five steps: ask the decision maker's question, agree in advance what result would change the decision, share early findings privately, publish a short brief at the moment of decision, stay available. **Tie evaluation to a fixed decision point.**
notes.69: Learn the 2005 design: a legal entitlement to not less than a hundred days, weekly or fortnightly wages, and an allowance if work was not given within fifteen days. The funding rule made it demand-driven: **the Union paid all unskilled wages**, so more demand meant more Union funding. Compare it with the new Act next.
notes.70: Read the new Act's four features: planning from Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans, four focus areas, a sixty-day seasonal pause notified by states, and a Centrally Sponsored Scheme funding split. The guarantee rises to 125 days. **Commencement was 1 July 2026**, three months before the deck's date. Check state Schemes for detail.
notes.71: Read the table row by row, since the change goes beyond the number of days. The funding rule, the allocation cap, the planning rule and the seasonal pause change **who decides how much work is available and when**. Use the statutes for a comparison like this, and read them yourself before relying on any summary.
notes.72: These four prompts are monitoring questions, and none is a finding. Ask whether work offered tracks demand or the allocation, whether the Scheme deadline and seasonal pause change availability, and which indicators will be published. **There is no full-year outcome data yet**, so any claim of effect is premature.
notes.73: Know the legal basis of DBT: the Aadhaar Act 2016, with section 7 allowing authentication as a condition for subsidies. The Supreme Court upheld section 7 and struck down the part of section 57 allowing private authentication. Note the **Money Bill** question: the majority accepted it and the dissent called it a fraud on the Constitution.
notes.74: This table sets four pieces of evidence side by side, and they point in different directions. The takeaway is at the foot: **track exclusion errors with the same care as leakage**. Compare the Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand rows to see that technology's effect depends on rollout design, and treat the PIB figure as a claim.
notes.75: BISP shows targeting as a political choice. First, forms were given to legislators; then a poverty scorecard based on a proxy means test replaced them. **Who identifies the poor decides who controls the programme.** Payments go to women in eligible households, and the scale figure comes from Pakistan's Economic Survey.
notes.76: Aswesuma replaced Samurdhi in 2023 under a loan condition and scores households on six dimensions. The appraisal says the weights and cut-off were not public. The lesson: **a formula can be more objective than discretion and still exclude**, if it is opaque and the appeal route is weak.
notes.77: Use the five lessons as design questions for any new scheme. Read across: who pays, who identifies beneficiaries, what happens when authentication fails, whether a household can see and appeal its score, and who has the budget and staff to comply with a court order. **Carry these questions into Section 10's checklist.**
notes.79: Technically sound policies fail when the losers are organised and attentive and the gainers are scattered. Keep two questions apart: the technical one asks which policy works best, and the political economy one asks who decides, gains, loses and responds. **BISP shows both at work**, the scorecard being the technical answer and its adoption the political choice.
notes.80: Use the three steps to keep the analysis focused: define the problem, examine governance and institutions, examine interests, incentives and power. Stop when you can explain the problem you need to solve. The example questions help: **which rule creates the bottleneck, and who benefits from it staying?**
notes.81: Place stakeholders by power and interest, and match engagement to the cell. Work through the invented plastic-ban map: engage high-power, high-interest actors early, keep high-power, low-interest ones satisfied, and organise and consult low-power, high-interest ones. The reminder to keep: **most consumers decide whether the ban works**.
notes.82: Use the rule of thumb: concentrated costs and diffuse benefits favour the small organised group. The LPG finding explains why untargeted subsidies persist, since better-off users notice any cut. Read the table by asking who sits on each side. **A reform needs a coalition designed to defend it.**
notes.83: A shared scheme has two sets of politicians with different incentives. Under 60:40 a state pays two rupees for every three from the Union, and credit may go to whichever level voters notice. Use the three watch-for items, and recall that **fewer resources go where responsibility is unclear**.
notes.84: Test every proposal on four kinds of feasibility: technical, political, administrative, financial. Write your judgement and evidence for each so others can challenge it. The warning at the foot is blunt: **administrative feasibility is the test most often skipped**, and Sections 6 and 8 show it failing most often.
notes.85: Timing matters as much as content, and you cannot open a window but can be ready for one. Preparation means evidence, a costed proposal, draft text and allies. Watch the signals: **new government, budget cycle, court hearing, crisis, new survey**. Prepare comments for a 30-day consultation before one arrives.
notes.87: Learn the six steps in order: define the problem, set criteria, build three or four options, project outcomes and costs, compare trade-offs, recommend. Two rules guard against bias. **Always include the status quo as an option**, and state criteria first, because choosing them after seeing results favours a preferred option.
notes.88: Do the eight checks before acting on a policy. Start with the parent Act and work through rules, Scheme, guidelines, budget line, court orders, committee reports, evaluations and a frontline official. The worked check shows **MGNREGA repealed with savings under s37** and state Schemes due within six months.
notes.89: Read the scoring table together with its final sentence. Adding scores is not the decision, since weights matter, and the scores here are invented. The team would favour the combined nominee and audited override if it weights exclusion highest. **State your weights explicitly** and plan the audit carefully.
notes.90: Match each stage to a formal route and a deliverable. Agenda setting needs evidence of size, formulation needs clause-specific comments, committees want a short memo, implementation needs RTI requests and records, review needs outcome evidence. **Informal relationships with the officer who holds the file matter at every stage.**
notes.91: Pick the monitoring rows that match the main risk, agree them before rollout, and set the early-warning sign in advance. The legal deadlines are natural indicators: **wages within a fortnight and work within fifteen days of an application**. Pair leakage monitoring with exclusion monitoring, as earlier sections require.
notes.92: Run this list as a final check before a recommendation leaves your desk. The analysis column warns against treating guidelines as law and counting leakage savings without exclusion. The engagement column warns about timing and targeting. **Write down the decision, the person and the date before you start.**
notes.94: A brief is short, usually two to four pages, and judged on whether it is used. Before writing, answer three questions in one sentence each: **who will read it, what decision they face, and what you want them to do**. The comparison with a research paper shows how the purposes differ.
notes.95: Put the conclusion first: a title that states the finding, a 100-word summary, the problem with numbers and sources, options including the status quo, a recommendation with next steps, then sources. Keep **two or three findings that matter for the decision**. A title that names a topic gives no finding.
notes.96: Rewrite your first draft against the before and after example. Lead each paragraph with its point, give every number a source and year, use the active voice and name who must act, and state uncertainty once with its reason. **'One in eight eligible families was refused rations'** shows the target style.
notes.97: Be exact about what is known. Give the source and year, say what kind of study produced the number, and state the main limit in a plain sentence. Show ranges when estimates differ. **Label invented examples as illustrative**, and date any claim that can change, such as a law's status.
notes.98: Treat the summary as a revision card. Each point links to a section and a decision, and the last line reminds you to check later amendments, rules and judgments. If you can state the **ten points in your own words**, you have the course. Test yourself by explaining one point to a colleague.
notes.99: Choose the next course by your concern. Start with Governance & Accountability 101 if implementation is your problem, or Political Economy 101 for the incentives behind policy choices. The list also covers law, budgets, advocacy, evaluation, programme design and data protection. **All courses are free.**
